title: My Substitute Teaching Was Saved by a Student's Wrong Answer
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer describes a humbling day substitute teaching math in Oakland, where the one bright spot was a student's incorrect answer on a Stacking Cups problem. By calling the answer brilliant and wrong, he turned an error into a shared puzzle about why a seemingly correct linear extrapolation fails. He argues that although math teachers recite slogans about mistakes being expected and respected, their practice often treats errors as problems, reinforcing perfectionism and paternalism. As a remedy, he proposes a pedagogy of generosity toward student thinking: for any question, predict the most common wrong answer, ask how it is brilliant, and decide what to do with it next. The piece is short and ends in a link roundup, but its central exercise is concrete and portable for teachers and teams planning lessons.
points: Naming a wrong answer as brilliant reframes mistakes as material for the whole class to reason about, not as personal failure.
Meyer argues that students watch what teachers do more than what posters or slogans say, so the mistakes-are-respected message must show up in practice.
Treating errors as problems to correct reinforces perfectionism and the idea that experts are the only ones who fix mistakes.
A usable planning routine: predict the likeliest wrong answer, find what is brilliant in it, and plan the next move.
quotes: The brightest spot of the day was when a student offered a wrong answer. I went from his desk to the front of the room and said to everyone, "Octavio has a really brilliant wrong answer I have to share with you.
We were working on Stacking Cups. The student saw that 5 cups was 15 centimeters tall and calculated that 10 cups would be 30 centimeters tall. But it isn’t. It’s 22 centimeters tall.

Though math teachers often tout the phrase “mistakes are expected, respected, inspected, and corrected,” their practices don’t always align. Teachers often treat mistakes as problems by equating them with wrongness, rather than treating them as opportunities for learning—which reinforces the ideas of perfectionism (that students shouldn’t make mistakes) and paternalism (teachers or other experts can and should correct mistakes).

As an exercise in developing a pedagogy of generosity towards student thinking, I highly recommend taking any math question and asking yourself (perhaps with colleagues) "What will be the most common wrong answer to this question? How is it brilliant? What can I do with it next?
Kids are watching what we do and how we teach, more than the words we say or the posters we put on the wall.

From the front of the room, I trusted a bunch of strangers and some of them seemed to trust me to help all of us figure out why an answer that seemed very correct was actually incorrect. We figured out why, and afterwards, we talked about a version of the situation where, had we stacked cups differently, Octavio's answer would have been correct.
